disease_resistance: Some tolerance to early blight; susceptible to late blight; prone to cracking if watering is inconsistent
companion_notes: Plant deep to encourage root growth. Add calcium (lime, eggshells, or bone meal) at planting to prevent blossom end rot. Rotate out of Solanaceae (tomato/pepper/eggplant/potato) for 4 years between plantings.
variety_notes: Heirloom from Tennessee. Seeds reportedly passed down through the Cherokee tribe. Introduced to commerce in 1990 by Craig LeHoullier. 12-16 oz dusky pink fruit with deep red-purple interior and green shoulders. Consistently wins taste tests. Yields ~20 fruits per plant. Vigorous vines require staking or caging.
sources: Victory Seeds; Bonnie Plants; Pinetree Garden Seeds; St. Clare Heirloom Seeds; Nature & Nurture Seeds; Almanac Planting
source_notes: Days to maturity varies by source based on whether counted from seed or transplant: 70-75 from transplant, 80-90 from seed. Used 70-90 to span both.

disease_resistance: Susceptible to most common tomato diseases; relatively demanding variety
companion_notes: Requires rich soil, consistent water, and patient growing. Rotate out of Solanaceae family for 4 years.
variety_notes: Classic Amish heirloom dating to 1880s from Chester County, PA. Potato-leaf foliage distinguishes the true Brandywine. Large 1-2 lb pink beefsteak fruits with rich, complex, sweet-tart flavor widely considered the benchmark for heirloom tomato flavor. Low yield (6-10 fruits per plant) but exceptional quality. Portland Nursery taste test rates 5/5 stars. Moderate disease resistance — prefers cooler climates.
sources: Johnny's Selected Seeds; Baker Creek; Seed Savers Exchange; Victory Seeds; Tomato Dirt; Home for the Harvest; Portland Nursery
source_notes: Brandywine has several strains (Sudduth's, OTV, Yellow, Red) — default referenced here is the classic pink strain.

disease_resistance: Resistant to fusarium wilt and tobacco mosaic virus; prone to cracking in wet weather
companion_notes: Heavy producer — pick frequently to maintain production. Thin interior foliage to prevent cracking.
variety_notes: F1 hybrid released by Tokita Seed Company (Japan). Widely considered the best-flavored cherry tomato — intensely sweet golden-orange fruit with tropical fruity notes. Crack-prone (pick at first sign of blush). Extremely productive all season. Fruit hangs in long trusses. Once tried, most gardeners grow it every year. NOTE: Open-pollinated Sunrise Bumble Bee and related varieties are often marketed as alternatives but don't match Sungold flavor.
sources: Johnny's Selected Seeds; Baker Creek; Territorial Seed; Totally Tomatoes; Sierra Vista Growers
source_notes: F1 hybrid — seeds won't come true from saved seed. Sungold's flavor is consistently cited as its defining feature.

disease_resistance: Prone to blossom end rot — maintain consistent watering and calcium; good general disease resistance
companion_notes: Requires consistent even watering to avoid blossom end rot. Mulch heavily. Rotate Solanaceae for 4 years.
variety_notes: Italian heirloom from volcanic soils near Mt. Vesuvius, in cultivation since the 16th century. DOP-protected Italian paste tomato — the benchmark sauce/pizza tomato. Long 3-4 oz plum-shaped fruit with pointed ends. Thick dry low-acid flesh with few seeds. Strips easily for peeling. "San Marzano II" is the widely-available improved strain. Note: eats bland fresh; shines when cooked. Highly susceptible to blossom end rot.
sources: High Mowing Seeds; Mary's Heirloom Seeds; David's Garden Seeds; The Gardener's Workshop; Thresh Seed Co
source_notes: Original San Marzano is a determinate variety; San Marzano II and other improved strains are mostly indeterminate. Specified indeterminate as the common available form.

disease_resistance: Better disease resistance than San Marzano; notably less prone to blossom end rot
companion_notes: Provide sturdy support — vines are vigorous and fruit-laden. Rotate out of Solanaceae for 4 years.
variety_notes: Heirloom originating in Wisconsin around 1870, discovered in Lancaster PA Amish community, commercialized 1990. Slow Food Ark of Taste listed. Large 8-12 oz oxheart/oblong paste tomato — twice the size of Roma. Meaty, few-seeded, coreless. Juicier and sweeter than San Marzano — excellent fresh AND for sauces. Portland Nursery rates flavor 4.4/5 vs San Marzano 3.3/5. Yields 20-40 lbs per plant; exceptional plants hit 99 lbs.
sources: Thresh Seed Co; Prairie Road Organic; Mary's Heirloom Seeds; Ask the Food Geek; Lee Reich
source_notes: Consistently rated best-flavored paste tomato by multiple sources. Strong recommendation for gardeners who want one dual-purpose paste/slicer.

disease_resistance: Resistant to verticillium wilt (V), fusarium wilt (F), and nematodes (N); some strains also resist late blight
companion_notes: Dense foliage protects fruit from sunscald. Rotate Solanaceae crops.
variety_notes: F1 hybrid bred in California in the 1960s — improved version of Big Boy. All-America Selections winner. 12-16 oz globe-shaped red slicer with classic balanced tomato flavor. Holds Guinness World Record (single plant produced 340+ lbs). Extremely reliable producer — dependable even in challenging conditions. Not suited for containers due to size. Indeterminate vines grow to 8-10 feet on strong support.
sources: Victory Seeds; Better Boy (Wikipedia); Sierra Vista Growers; Gardening Know How; Home for the Harvest; David's Garden Seeds
source_notes: Reliable reliable workhorse hybrid — recommended over heirlooms for beginner gardeners who want consistent yields.

disease_resistance: Resistant to verticillium wilt (V) and fusarium wilt (F)
companion_notes: Rotate out of Solanaceae. Water deeply and consistently for best fruit quality.
variety_notes: F1 hybrid popular for short-season areas and impatient gardeners. Among the earliest-maturing slicers at 50-60 days. Medium 4-8 oz red round fruit with good tangy flavor. Reliable producer in cooler/northern climates. Often the first tomato to ripen in the garden. Pairs well with later-ripening heirlooms to extend harvest season.
sources: Burpee; Baker Creek; Johnny's Selected Seeds; Territorial Seed
source_notes: Standard early variety — reliable data across sources.

disease_resistance: Tobacco Mosaic Virus resistance (TMR) in improved strains like California Wonder 300 TMR
companion_notes: Rotate out of Solanaceae family for 3-4 years. Interplant with basil or tomatoes for companion benefits. Plant when nights reach 60F.
variety_notes: Heirloom introduced in 1928 — established the standard for American bell peppers. Large thick-walled 4-inch blocky 4-lobed fruit — excellent for stuffing. Green when immature, ripens to sweet red. 0 Scoville (no heat — capsaicinoid pathway switched off). Yields 6-8 peppers per plant. Classic choice for home gardens. California Wonder 300 TMR is the improved Tobacco Mosaic-resistant strain widely sold today.
sources: Plant Addicts; Urban Farmer; Botanical Interests; Thresh Seed Co; PepperScale; Mint2Grow
source_notes: 1928 introduction date and thick walls for stuffing are defining features.

disease_resistance: Generally hardy; some strains resist TMV; widely adaptable
companion_notes: Rotate Solanaceae. Good companion for basil, carrots, cucumbers, eggplants, oregano, parsley. Avoid planting near beans, cabbage, kale, fennel.
variety_notes: Named for Jalapa, Mexico — the most popular chile pepper in the United States. 3-inch thick-walled moderately hot pods with deep green color maturing to red. 2,500-8,000 Scoville heat units (SHU) — the reference point on the heat scale. Heat varies even on the same plant: stressed plants produce hotter fruit. Widely adaptable in dry/humid and hot/cool climates. Excellent in containers. Smoked red ones = chipotle. First pepper in space (1982).
sources: Bonnie Plants; PepperScale; True Leaf Market; Wildrose Heritage
source_notes: 2,500-8,000 SHU is the standard reference point used across all pepper scale comparisons.

disease_resistance: Prone to blossom end rot (add lime at transplanting); susceptible to Tobacco Mosaic Virus
companion_notes: Lime at planting to prevent blossom end rot. Consistent watering essential. Harvest frequently to encourage continued production.
variety_notes: Japanese heirloom — a cultivar of the Spanish Padrón pepper. Name from "shishi" (lion). Thin-walled wrinkled 2-4 inch green pepper ripens to red. 50-200 SHU typically — the "Shishito roulette" means roughly 1 in 10 fruits can hit 1,000 SHU unexpectedly (still mild vs Jalapeño). Most-often eaten green, grilled/fried whole as appetizer with sea salt. Fast to mature from transplant. Highly productive — pick often.
sources: Gardening Chores; Cultivated Earth; Thresh Seed Co
source_notes: Shishito heat variability is a defining feature — environmental stress increases capsaicin production.

disease_resistance: TMV-resistant strains available (Trident); generally hardy in warm climates
companion_notes: Plant 3-4 feet from other plants — they grow LARGE. Rotate Solanaceae for 3-4 years.
variety_notes: Mexican heirloom from Puebla region. Same pepper, two names: POBLANO when fresh green (fresh use, stuffed for chiles rellenos), ANCHO when dried (deep brick red, used for chili powder and mole). 4-5 inch broad slightly flattened heart-shaped fruit. 1,000-1,500 SHU — mild heat, rich earthy sweet flavor with smoky notes when dried. Flavor deepens and heat increases as fruit ripens from green to red on plant. Substitute when recipes call for Jalapeño and you want less heat.
sources: Victory Seeds; Bonnie Plants; Fedco; John Scheepers; PepperScale; White Harvest; Annies Heirloom
source_notes: Green/red + fresh/dried name distinction (Poblano vs Ancho) is a common point of confusion for home cooks.

disease_resistance: Generally disease resistant; prefers hot humid conditions
companion_notes: Needs 100+ days of full sun. Start indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost. WEAR GLOVES when handling ripe fruit — capsaicin oil burns skin.
variety_notes: Native to Yucatan, Mexico. Thin-walled 1-1.5 inch wrinkled lantern-shaped fruit ripens from green to golden orange (or red, chocolate, white). 100,000-350,000 SHU — among the hottest common peppers (1,000x hotter than Jalapeño reference). Fruity citrus flavor with floral aroma beneath the intense heat. Long growing season — needs heat. Often grown as perennial in zones 9-11. Essential for Caribbean sauces and Yucatecan cuisine.
sources: Smart Gardener; MasterClass; True Leaf Market
source_notes: Heat level and the 1000x-jalapeno comparison are key orientation facts for casual users.

disease_resistance: Generally hardy; susceptible to powdery mildew in humid conditions
companion_notes: Good companion for basil, carrots, cucumbers, oregano, parsley. Avoid fennel and kohlrabi. Stake as needed.
variety_notes: Second-most-popular Mexican pepper after Jalapeño. Smaller (3-4 inch) and thinner than Jalapeño but HOTTER — 8,000-23,000 SHU (3-10x Jalapeño). Bright fresh grassy flavor with juicy flesh. Essential for authentic pico de gallo, salsa, and guacamole. Ripens green to red (also orange/yellow/brown variants). Cut with scissors to harvest — delicate stems. Produces heavily once started.
sources: Pepper Joe's; Bank on Seeds; Gardeners Basics; MasterClass; Gardener's Path; OSC Seeds
source_notes: Heat roughly 3x hotter than Jalapeño — important calibration when substituting in recipes.

disease_resistance: Heat and humidity tolerant; generally pest-resistant
companion_notes: Tolerates hot humid weather better than most peppers. Good in containers. Harvest full-size for full heat.
variety_notes: Long thin 5-6 inch wrinkled red chili. 30,000-50,000 SHU — significantly hotter than Jalapeño and Serrano. Won't be hot when small — must reach full 5-6 inch size. Primary ingredient in Cayenne powder (dried, ground). Essential for Creole and Cajun cooking (gumbo, crayfish). Can substitute for Serrano, Jalapeño, or Habanero depending on heat desired. Produces all summer; tolerant of hot humid weather.
sources: Bonnie Plants; True Leaf Market; Wildrose Heritage
source_notes: Heat builds as peppers mature — pick small for milder flavor, full-size for full heat.

disease_resistance: Susceptible to downy mildew and fusarium wilt — look for resistant strains (Prospera series, Nufar, Aroma 2)
companion_notes: Classic companion for tomatoes — plant together for mutual benefit. Pinch growing tips at 4-6" tall to encourage bushing. Damaged by temperatures below 50F.
variety_notes: Italian heirloom originating near Genoa. THE traditional pesto basil. Large dark green glossy spoon-shaped leaves with sweet peppery flavor and notes of anise, clove, and mint. Slow to bolt in heat and doesn't become bitter with age. More aromatic than generic sweet basil. Harvest full plant 4-6" above ground just before flowering for second growth. Flowers are edible and intensely flavored.
sources: Johnny's Selected Seeds; Fedco; High Mowing Seeds; Urban Farmer; Gardener's Path; Gardening Know How
source_notes: Improved strains (Prospera, Nufar) have better disease resistance than classic Genovese.

disease_resistance: Less susceptible to downy mildew than sweet basil — good choice for humid climates
companion_notes: Same companion rules as other basils. Consistent moisture and heat needed.
variety_notes: Distinct from sweet (Genovese) and holy basil — Thai basil has a spicy anise/licorice flavor essential for authentic Thai, Vietnamese, and Malaysian cuisine. Purple stems and flower spikes. Narrower pointed leaves. Siam Queen is the most popular cultivar — 1997 All-America Selections winner. Seeds have lower germination (~75%) — plant extra. Holds up to stir-fry heat better than sweet basil.
sources: Gardener's Path; Johnny's Selected Seeds
source_notes: Three main basil categories: sweet (O. basilicum), Thai (var. thyrsiflora), holy/tulsi (O. tenuiflorum) — different species entirely.

plant_type: tender perennial (grown as annual in cold climates)
disease_resistance: More drought and pest resistant than sweet basil
companion_notes: Sacred in Hindu tradition — often grown near homes. Very attractive to pollinators.
variety_notes: Different species (Ocimum tenuiflorum) from sweet and Thai basils. Hint of clove and citrus. Sacred herb in Hindu Ayurvedic tradition — used for tea rather than culinary dishes. Three main types: Rama (green), Krishna (purple), Vana (wild). More drought-tolerant than sweet basil. Attractive to bees and butterflies.
sources: Gardener's Path; Johnny's Selected Seeds
source_notes: Primarily a medicinal/tea herb rather than culinary.

start_method: cutting or transplant (seed slow and unreliable)
disease_resistance: Drought tolerant; disease resistant once established. Avoid wet feet — root rot is primary killer
companion_notes: Classic companion for cabbage, beans, carrots. Repels bean beetles and carrot flies. Loves sandy well-drained soil.
variety_notes: Hardiest rosemary variety — survives zone 6 winters (-10F) where typical rosemary dies. Selected in Arp, Texas. Excellent culinary flavor — piney and resinous. Grow in full sun with sharp drainage — wet clay soil kills it. Prune regularly to prevent legginess. Tolerates heat and drought once established.
sources: Johnny's Selected Seeds; Richters Herbs; Mountain Valley Growers
source_notes: Zone 6 hardiness is the defining feature — most rosemary is zone 7+.

disease_resistance: Very drought tolerant; disease resistant. Rejuvenate every 3-4 years by dividing or replacing
companion_notes: Great companion for cabbage family (repels cabbage worms), eggplant, strawberries. Drought-tolerant — ideal for rock gardens.
variety_notes: The classic culinary thyme. Small gray-green leaves with warm earthy flavor. Hardy in zone 4-5 with snow cover. Excellent for Mediterranean cuisine, roasted meats, bouquet garni. Harvest before flowering for peak flavor. Easy to propagate from cuttings. Gets woody over time — replace every 3-4 years.
sources: Johnny's Selected Seeds; Richters Herbs; Burpee
source_notes: Hardy and forgiving — great beginner perennial herb.

disease_resistance: Drought tolerant; disease resistant; minimal pest issues
companion_notes: Excellent companion for peppers, tomatoes, and brassicas. Attracts beneficial insects and pollinators when flowering.
variety_notes: The TRUE culinary oregano with strong pungent flavor — essential distinction from common Origanum vulgare (sold generically as "oregano") which is far less flavorful. Small fuzzy gray-green leaves with white flowers. Hardy zone 4+. Spreads slowly. Harvest just before flowering for peak potency. Dried oregano has stronger flavor than fresh — one of few herbs this is true for.
sources: Johnny's Selected Seeds; Mountain Valley Growers; Richters Herbs
source_notes: Subspecies hirtum (Greek) is distinct from common oregano — flavor difference is dramatic.

disease_resistance: Drought and heat tolerant; minimal pest issues; root rot in wet soil
companion_notes: Good with rosemary, cabbage family, carrots, strawberries. Repels cabbage moths and carrot flies. Avoid planting near cucumbers.
variety_notes: Essential herb for stuffings, poultry, sausage, and Italian dishes. Gray-green velvety leaves with strong savory flavor. Purple flowers attract pollinators. Pine well-drained neutral-to-alkaline soil. Becomes woody after 3-5 years — replace for best flavor. Prune back hard after flowering. Drought tolerant once established.
sources: Johnny's Selected Seeds; Burpee; Richters Herbs
source_notes: Purple, golden, and tricolor varieties available but common green sage has best culinary flavor.

start_method: transplant or cutting (don't start from seed — runners spread quickly)
disease_resistance: Very hardy; mint rust can occur in humid conditions
companion_notes: PLANT IN CONTAINERS OR CONTAINED BEDS — mint spreads aggressively via underground runners and will take over any garden. Good companion if contained: repels ants, aphids, cabbage moths.
variety_notes: THE kitchen mint for mojitos, mint juleps, lamb, tabbouleh, and mint tea. Bright fresh clean flavor vs peppermint's menthol intensity. Spreads aggressively — grow in bottomless containers sunk in garden, or dedicated contained beds. Pinch flowers for best leaf flavor. Harvest often to keep fresh growth coming.
sources: Burpee; Johnny's Selected Seeds; Richters Herbs
source_notes: Aggressive spreading behavior is the critical warning for home gardeners.

start_method: indoor start (slow to germinate) or direct sow
disease_resistance: Generally pest-resistant; host plant for swallowtail butterfly caterpillars (leave them to feed)
companion_notes: Excellent companion for tomatoes, asparagus, corn. Attracts beneficial wasps that prey on pest insects.
variety_notes: Stronger flavor than curly parsley — preferred by cooks. Bright fresh flavor with slight pepperiness. Soak seeds 24 hours before planting to speed germination. Slow to germinate (2-4 weeks). Biennial: grows leaves year 1, flowers and dies year 2. Harvest outer stems at base to keep producing. Hardy through light frosts.
sources: Johnny's Selected Seeds; Burpee; Territorial Seed
source_notes: Flat-leaf vs curly is essentially a flavor preference — flat-leaf is stronger.

sun_requirement: full sun to part shade (part shade in summer)
disease_resistance: Generally pest-resistant; bolts quickly in heat — that's the main issue
companion_notes: Good companion for tomatoes, spinach, basil. Attracts beneficial insects when flowering. Avoid planting near fennel.
variety_notes: BOLTS QUICKLY IN HOT WEATHER — succession plant every 2-3 weeks for continuous supply. "Santo" is the slow-bolt variety best suited for summer. Leaves = cilantro; seeds = coriander (harvest dry seeds when plant bolts — saves seed for next crop). Essential in Mexican, Thai, Indian cuisine. ~10-20% of people perceive cilantro as soapy due to genetic variation in olfactory receptors.
sources: Johnny's Selected Seeds; Burpee; Territorial Seed
source_notes: Bolting in heat is THE challenge with cilantro — succession planting is essential.

start_method: direct sow or transplant (slow from seed)
disease_resistance: Very hardy; minimal pest issues; repels aphids and carrot flies
companion_notes: Plant throughout the garden to repel aphids, Japanese beetles, and carrot flies. Great companion for carrots, roses, and tomatoes. Divide clumps every 3-4 years to maintain vigor.
variety_notes: Hardiest allium — grows year-round in most climates, returns reliably from roots. Mild onion flavor — great fresh in salads, baked potatoes, eggs, soft cheese. Edible purple pompom flowers — sprinkle on salads. Cut back in mid-season for a fresh flush of tender leaves. Divide clumps every 3-4 years.
sources: Johnny's Selected Seeds; Burpee; Territorial Seed
source_notes: Zone 3 hardiness makes it one of the toughest culinary perennials.

disease_resistance: Generally pest-free; host plant for swallowtail butterflies
companion_notes: Great companion for cabbage family (brassicas) and cucumbers. Attracts beneficial wasps and butterflies. Avoid planting near carrots (can cross-pollinate). Self-seeds readily if allowed to flower.
variety_notes: Most popular home garden dill. Leaves ready at 40-55 days; seeds ready at ~90 days. Harvest leaves ("dill weed") for fresh use and pickling; harvest seed heads for pickling brines and spice. Bolts quickly — succession plant every 3 weeks for continuous leaf supply, or let a few go to seed for future crops (self-seeds prolifically). Cannot be transplanted — direct sow only.
sources: Johnny's Selected Seeds; Burpee; Territorial Seed
source_notes: Self-seeding means one planting can provide dill for years.

sun_requirement: full sun to part shade (shade in summer)
disease_resistance: Some resistance to tipburn; more heat-tolerant than typical butterhead; bolts in high heat
companion_notes: Great companion for carrots, radishes, strawberries. Protect from hot afternoon sun.
variety_notes: All-America Selections winner 1963. The classic Bibb-type butterhead — loose heads of tender buttery green leaves with a slight crunch. More heat-tolerant than most butterheads. Excellent for salads and sandwiches. Succession-plant every 2-3 weeks spring and fall. Cool-season crop — struggles above 75F. Cut outer leaves or harvest whole head.
sources: Wildrose Heritage; Live Better Garden; Johnny's Selected Seeds; Burpee
source_notes: Heat tolerance is the defining feature — outperforms generic butterheads in early-summer garden.

disease_resistance: Resistance to tip burn; tolerance to mosaic virus; medium bolt resistance
companion_notes: Romaine is more heat-tolerant than most lettuces — good for extending the season into summer.
variety_notes: Classic heirloom dark-green romaine — the benchmark home garden romaine. 10-12" upright heads with slightly savoyed dark green leaves and creamy yellow heart. THE lettuce for Caesar salads. Tolerates heat better than butterhead or leaf lettuces. Good resistance to tipburn and mosaic virus.
sources: Wildrose Heritage; High Mowing Seeds; Blue Pumpkin Seed Co; Heirloom Organics
source_notes: Very adaptable and forgiving — excellent beginner romaine.

disease_resistance: Heat resistant, slow to bolt for a leaf lettuce
companion_notes: Cool-season crop — plant early spring and fall. Keep soil moist for best flavor.
variety_notes: 150+ year old heirloom — still one of the most popular leaf lettuces. Fast-growing bright-green frilly leaves with tender texture and delicate flavor. "Cut-and-come-again" — harvest outer leaves and plant keeps producing. Baby greens ready in 28 days; full harvest at 45-50. Well-adapted to wide range of climates.
sources: Wildrose Heritage; Pinetree Garden Seeds; Live Better Garden; Burpee
source_notes: The heritage loose-leaf benchmark — essentially the "basic" home garden lettuce.

disease_resistance: Slow to bolt — more heat-tolerant than many loose-leaf types
companion_notes: Mix with darker lettuces for color contrast. Cut-and-come-again harvesting.
variety_notes: Deeply lobed oak-shaped leaves. Green Oakleaf and Red Oakleaf are both widely grown. Slow to bolt in heat — one of the best leaf lettuces for extending the season. Sweet mild flavor. Excellent for salad mixes. Beautiful garden ornamental as well as edible.
sources: Johnny's Selected Seeds; Baker Creek; Territorial Seed
source_notes: "Oakleaf" refers to a leaf shape category with multiple specific cultivars (Salad Bowl, Red Salad Bowl, etc).

disease_resistance: Good resistance to downy mildew and tipburn; disease-resistant breeding program
companion_notes: Premium variety bred specifically for one-cut harvest — ideal for market gardeners or home growers wanting salad-ready heads.
variety_notes: Modern premium breeding line (multiple colors and shapes in the Salanova series). Single core cut at base releases a pre-portioned salad of small uniform leaves. Highly productive. Excellent baby-leaf quality. Heat-tolerant. Commonly grown by market gardeners but excellent for home gardens too. Available in butterhead, oakleaf, and incised-leaf types, in green and red.
sources: Johnny's Selected Seeds; Territorial Seed
source_notes: Salanova is a trademark line — seed is more expensive than open-pollinated lettuces but performance is superior.

start_method: direct sow after frost or indoor start
disease_resistance: Resistant to scab, cucumber mosaic virus, downy mildew, powdery mildew — the standard disease-resistant slicer
companion_notes: Good companion for corn, beans, radishes, sunflowers. Avoid planting near sage or potatoes. Keep evenly watered to prevent bitterness.
variety_notes: Developed by Cornell University — the most widely-grown slicing cucumber in the Northeast. Dark green smooth 8-9" straight non-bitter fruits. Exceptional disease resistance. Productive until frost. Vining habit — trellis for easier harvest and cleaner fruit. Bitter-free genetics. The default slicer variety.
sources: Johnny's Selected Seeds; High Mowing Seeds; Burpee; Wildrose Heritage
source_notes: Cornell breeding makes this the disease-resistance gold standard.

disease_resistance: Resistant to cucumber mosaic virus; good general disease resistance
companion_notes: Harvest frequently at 2-6" long for best pickling quality. Missing fruits trigger plant to stop producing.
variety_notes: Introduced 1924 — THE classic pickling cucumber. Dark green cylindrical 5-7" fruits with black spines. Heavy yielder. Perfect ratio of skin to flesh for crisp pickles. Harvest at 2-4" for gherkins, 4-6" for standard dill pickles. Pick every 1-2 days during peak production to keep plant producing.
sources: Wildrose Heritage; Baker Creek; True Leaf Market
source_notes: The classic American pickling cucumber.

disease_resistance: Good general disease resistance; productive in hot climates
companion_notes: Trellis for cleanest fruit. Harvest when pale yellow — over-ripe fruits turn deep yellow and can be bitter.
variety_notes: Heirloom dating to 1894. Round 2-3" lemon-shaped and pale yellow fruits. Sweet mild non-bitter flesh with tender edible skin. Productive even in hot dry conditions. Novelty appeal plus excellent flavor — great for kids. Pick at pale-yellow stage; too-yellow fruits go bitter. Perfect snacking size.
sources: Baker Creek; Johnny's Selected Seeds; Territorial Seed
source_notes: Reliable heirloom that performs in climates where standard cucumbers struggle.

disease_resistance: More heat-tolerant and less disease-prone than true cucumbers — excellent for hot climates
companion_notes: Must be trellised — fruits grow straight when hanging, curl into S-shapes on ground. Vigorous vines need strong support.
variety_notes: Technically a melon (Cucumis melo) not a true cucumber — but grown and eaten as one. Long pale green ribbed fruits 18-36 inches at full size. Mild sweet never-bitter flavor. Heat-tolerant where true cucumbers struggle. Harvest at 12-15" for best texture. Never needs peeling. Seeds tiny and edible.
sources: Baker Creek; Johnny's Selected Seeds; Botanical Interests
source_notes: Not technically Cucumis sativus — worth noting for seed-saving purposes.

disease_resistance: Moderate disease resistance
companion_notes: Pick every 2-3 days when producing. Cut fruit from vine rather than pulling to prevent vine damage.
variety_notes: 1935 All-America Selections winner. Classic smooth straight dark green 8" cucumbers with rounded blunt ends. Reliable and productive heirloom. Sweet mild flavor. Excellent for slicing. An American garden staple for nearly 90 years.
sources: Wildrose Heritage; Burpee; Baker Creek
source_notes: Reliable classic — a sensible default for beginners.

disease_resistance: Resistant to bean mosaic virus; tolerates cooler soil than most beans — germinates at 60F
companion_notes: Classic companion for corn, squash, cucumber. Adds nitrogen to soil. Avoid planting near onion/garlic family.
variety_notes: Earliest bush green bean. Germinates well in cool soil (60F) where other beans fail. Straight 5-6" round dark green pods. Reliable heavy producer. Harvest when pods snap cleanly. Succession plant every 2-3 weeks for continuous supply. Widely recommended for short-season gardens.
sources: Johnny's Selected Seeds; Territorial Seed; Fedco
source_notes: Standard early bush bean — very dependable.

disease_resistance: Resistant to common bean mosaic virus and powdery mildew; heat-tolerant
companion_notes: Three Sisters companion (corn + squash + beans). Good nitrogen fixer.
variety_notes: 1949 introduction, AAS winner. Heat-tolerant bush bean — keeps producing in hot weather where others stop. Tender stringless 6-7" medium-green pods. Heavy yielder. Excellent flavor. One of the most widely recommended bush beans.
sources: Johnny's Selected Seeds; Wildrose Heritage; Baker Creek
source_notes: Heat tolerance distinguishes Contender from other bush beans.

disease_resistance: Generally disease-resistant
companion_notes: Three Sisters companion. Purple streaks disappear when cooked — use fresh for visual appeal.
variety_notes: Dutch heirloom. Stunning pale yellow pods with bright purple streaks. Flat wax-bean type. Excellent snap bean flavor fresh; dries well as shell bean. Purple streaks disappear when cooked. Dual-purpose: eat young as snap bean or mature as shell/dry bean. Productive. Ornamental as well as delicious.
sources: Johnny's Selected Seeds; Baker Creek
source_notes: Popular dual-purpose heirloom; striking visual appeal.

start_method: direct sow at base of trellis
disease_resistance: Resistant to rust; good general disease resistance
companion_notes: MUST be trellised — needs 6-8 foot support. Good climber for Three Sisters plantings on corn.
variety_notes: Heirloom dating to 1864 — pre-Civil War variety. Old Homestead / Kentucky Wonder classic pole bean. 7-9" green pods with old-fashioned rich "beany" flavor that many consider the best of any green bean. Very productive — single planting provides all season. Heavy yields over extended harvest window. Strings somewhat as it matures — pick young and tender.
sources: Wildrose Heritage; Baker Creek; Johnny's Selected Seeds
source_notes: Flavor classic — many gardeners prefer this over modern stringless varieties.

disease_resistance: Resistant to common bean mosaic virus
companion_notes: Trellis with strong support. Good companion for corn (classic Three Sisters).
variety_notes: Originally bred in Oregon. Stringless 6-7" round dark green pods with tender flesh and rich bean flavor. Heavy producer. Slightly earlier than Kentucky Wonder. Excellent fresh, frozen, and canned. Classic commercial variety for good reason. Pole form is heavy yielder; bush form also available (Blue Lake 274) with different traits.
sources: Johnny's Selected Seeds; Territorial Seed; Baker Creek
source_notes: Blue Lake pole and bush are different varieties — pole generally higher yielding over longer season.

disease_resistance: Generally disease-resistant
companion_notes: Bright red flowers attract hummingbirds and bees. Ornamental edible — great on trellises or arbors as visual feature.
variety_notes: Different species from common beans (P. coccineus vs P. vulgaris). Stunning bright scarlet flowers attract hummingbirds all season. Young pods edible green (7-12" long); mature pinto-like beans excellent as shelled or dried beans. In zones 7+, roots may survive winter and regrow. Traditional English garden plant. Can be grown purely ornamentally for flowers.
sources: Johnny's Selected Seeds; Baker Creek; Territorial Seed
source_notes: Distinct species — cannot cross with common beans, useful for seed savers.

disease_resistance: Susceptible to squash bugs, vine borers, powdery mildew in late season
companion_notes: Classic Three Sisters planting with corn and beans. Plant nasturtiums nearby to repel pests. Harvest daily once production starts.
variety_notes: 1957 AAS winner. Glossy dark green fruits. THE classic American zucchini. Harvest at 6-8" for best flavor — lets fruit get to baseball bat size only if you want seeds. Single plant produces 10-20 lbs in season. Male and female flowers on same plant — first 1-2 weeks of bloom are male only (no fruit until female flowers appear).
sources: Johnny's Selected Seeds; Burpee; Baker Creek; Botanical Interests
source_notes: Famously productive — 2-3 plants feeds a family.

disease_resistance: Standard squash family susceptibility
companion_notes: Lower yields than Black Beauty but superior flavor compensates for home gardeners.
variety_notes: Italian heirloom prized by chefs and cookbook authors. Ribbed pale green fruits with nutty rich flavor — widely considered the best-flavored summer squash. Dense flesh doesn't get watery when cooked. Lower yielding (~50% of Black Beauty) but each fruit is delicious. Star-shaped cross-section. Male flowers abundant for stuffing and frying.
sources: Johnny's Selected Seeds; Baker Creek; Seed Savers Exchange
source_notes: Flavor-first variety — choose over productivity-first varieties like Black Beauty for home gardens.

disease_resistance: Standard summer squash susceptibility to vine borers, powdery mildew, squash bugs
companion_notes: Harvest young and often — 4-6" for best flavor and tender skin.
variety_notes: Traditional Southern US heirloom. Yellow fruits with curved neck and bumpy/warted skin at maturity. Sweet buttery flavor when harvested young (4-6"). Gets tough and seedy if allowed to grow too large. Classic for Southern cooking — squash casseroles, fritters. Pick at least every other day when producing.
sources: Baker Creek; Southern Exposure Seed Exchange
source_notes: Classic Southern heirloom — essential for Southern cuisine.

disease_resistance: Cucurbita moschata species is RESISTANT to squash vine borer (unlike C. pepo) — major advantage
companion_notes: Vine borer resistance makes moschata species (butternut, tromboncino, seminole) the best winter squash for borer-prone areas. Cure 10-14 days in sun after harvest for long storage.
variety_notes: 1970 AAS winner, developed at Waltham, Massachusetts. THE benchmark butternut — sweet tan-colored pear-shaped fruits with deep orange flesh. 4-5 lb fruits. Long-keeping (4-6 months at room temp properly cured). Excellent for soups, roasting, baking. Vigorous vines spread 10-15 feet. Harvest when rinds are hard and stem starts to dry. Uses curing period for maximum sweetness.
sources: Johnny's Selected Seeds; Wildrose Heritage; High Mowing Seeds; Burpee
source_notes: Vine borer resistance (species-level trait) is THE reason moschata squash are home garden favorites in borer regions.

disease_resistance: Susceptible to squash vine borer (like other C. pepo); good powdery mildew resistance in some strains
companion_notes: Storage life only 3 months — use up first before butternut. Eat skin and all — no peeling needed.
variety_notes: Heirloom revived from near-extinction in 1990s. 6-9" oblong cream-colored fruits with green stripes. Sweet rich flavor — often called "sweet potato squash." Thin edible skin — no peeling required. Shorter storage than butternut (3 months vs 6). Compact plants fit smaller gardens. Gaining popularity for its ease of preparation.
sources: Johnny's Selected Seeds; Baker Creek; Territorial Seed
source_notes: Near-extinction rescue — now mainstream popular variety.

disease_resistance: Susceptible to squash vine borer
companion_notes: Moderate storage — use within 2-3 months. Often halved and baked or stuffed.
variety_notes: 1913 heirloom from Des Moines, Iowa. Dark green ribbed acorn-shaped fruits with orange-yellow flesh. Mild sweet flavor. 1-3 lb fruits — perfect serving size when halved. Classic baking squash. Bush forms (Table Ace, Honey Bear) available for smaller gardens.
sources: Johnny's Selected Seeds; Burpee; Baker Creek
source_notes: Multiple named strains and hybrids available — Table Queen is the original heirloom.

disease_resistance: Susceptible to squash vine borer
companion_notes: Stores 1-2 months. Unique texture — flesh separates into spaghetti-like strands when cooked.
variety_notes: Originally from China via Japan. Oval tan-yellow fruit about 8-10" long, 2-4 lbs. When baked, flesh pulls into long spaghetti-like strands — substitute for pasta in low-carb cooking. Mild flavor. Harvest when skin is hard and color turns yellow. A unique novelty squash with serious culinary utility.
sources: Johnny's Selected Seeds; Burpee; Baker Creek
source_notes: The low-carb pasta substitute — entire market niche based on texture.

disease_resistance: Moderately resistant to diseases; watch for onion maggots and thrips
companion_notes: LONG-DAY onion (needs 14-16 hr daylight to bulb) — plant in northern tier (zones 5-8). Do NOT plant in the South — will not bulb properly. Good companion for carrots, beets, brassicas, tomatoes. Bad for beans and peas.
variety_notes: Sweet mild short-storage onion. Large flat-topped fruits, white to yellow skin. Brought from Corsica to Walla Walla, WA in late 1800s. Lower sulfur content = sweeter flavor + shorter storage (use within 1-2 months). Classic Pacific Northwest sweet onion. Direct replacement for Vidalia in northern gardens.
sources: Johnny's Selected Seeds; Territorial Seed; Baker Creek
source_notes: CRITICAL: day-length sensitivity is the single most important onion planting fact. Wrong latitude = no bulbs.

disease_resistance: Good general disease resistance
companion_notes: DAY-NEUTRAL / INTERMEDIATE-DAY onion — works in most US latitudes (not extreme north or south). Most flexible onion for zones 5-7.
variety_notes: Sweet mild yellow onion with medium-large round bulbs. Day-neutral — one of the few onions that works across wide latitude range. Adaptable to zones 5-7. Shorter storage than long-day onions (2-3 months). Popular for home gardeners who don't know their day-length category.
sources: Johnny's Selected Seeds; Territorial Seed
source_notes: Day-neutral flexibility is the selling point for home gardeners uncertain about day-length.

disease_resistance: Moderate disease resistance
companion_notes: SHORT-DAY onion (10-12 hours) — plant in southern tier (zones 7-10, south of 35N latitude). Will not bulb in the north.
variety_notes: Popular short-day red onion — the "Southern onion" choice. Deep red-purple globe-shaped bulbs with mild sweet flavor. 3-4 inch bulbs. Short storage (1-2 months). Best for fresh eating, salads, grilling. Plant in fall in the South for summer harvest.
sources: Baker Creek; Burpee; Territorial Seed
source_notes: Short-day category limits it to southern US — critical planting factor.

disease_resistance: Moderate disease resistance
companion_notes: LONG-DAY onion — plant in northern tier (zones 5-8). Better storage than Walla Walla — 3-4 months.
variety_notes: Classic heirloom long-day yellow onion. Large 4-6 inch globe-shaped bulbs with mild sweet flavor. Best storage of the sweet onions (3-4 months). Reliable producer across the North. Essential for canning, sautéing, and storage.
sources: Johnny's Selected Seeds; Burpee; Baker Creek
source_notes: Good balance of sweetness and storage — the workhorse long-day onion.

disease_resistance: Good general disease resistance when rotated properly
companion_notes: Plant cloves 2" deep, pointed end up, in fall 4-6 weeks before hard freeze. Mulch heavily over winter. HARDNECK type: cut scapes (flower stalks) in June for bigger bulbs. Harvest when 4-5 lower leaves have browned (usually July).
variety_notes: Most popular hardneck garlic. Porcelain type with 4-5 large easy-to-peel cloves per bulb. Rich robust garlic flavor with lingering heat. Excellent cold-hardiness (zone 3). Large bulbs (2-3 inches). Hardnecks produce edible scapes (flower stalks) — a bonus harvest in early summer. Shorter storage (6 months) than softnecks but superior flavor.
sources: Territorial Seed; Johnny's Selected Seeds; Filaree Garlic Farm
source_notes: Hardneck vs softneck distinction: hardneck = cold hardy + better flavor + scapes + shorter storage; softneck = warm climate + longer storage + braidable.

disease_resistance: Very hardy; good general disease resistance
companion_notes: Extremely cold-hardy — reliable choice for zone 3-4 growers.
variety_notes: Porcelain hardneck with 4-5 very large cloves per white bulb. Strong rich garlic flavor — one of the best-flavored hardnecks. Excellent cold tolerance (zone 3). Large uniform bulbs. Stores 6-8 months — longer than most hardnecks. Another top pick for northern gardeners.
sources: Filaree Garlic Farm; Territorial Seed
source_notes: Among the hardiest garlic varieties.

disease_resistance: Good general disease resistance
companion_notes: Softneck type — can be braided for storage hanging. No scapes to cut.
variety_notes: Artichoke-type softneck from Colville Indian Reservation in Washington. Rich mellow garlic flavor — won a 1990 Rodale Research taste test. 8-20 small-medium cloves per bulb. Excellent storage (9-12 months). Softneck = can be braided. More heat-tolerant than hardnecks — grows well zones 6-9.
sources: Filaree Garlic Farm; Territorial Seed; Baker Creek
source_notes: Best-tasting softneck per many growers.

disease_resistance: Good general disease resistance
companion_notes: Hardneck type — cut scapes in June, harvest bulbs in July.
variety_notes: Purple-Stripe hardneck from Shvelisi, Republic of Georgia. 8-10 purple-blushed cloves per bulb. Rated the BEST garlic for roasting — mellow deep flavor sweetens and becomes creamy when baked. Excellent raw flavor too. 6-month storage. Beautiful purple-striped bulbs.
sources: Filaree Garlic Farm; Territorial Seed
source_notes: Considered the top roasting garlic.

disease_resistance: Susceptible to cabbage worms, aphids, and flea beetles; generally hardy
companion_notes: Cold-hardy — flavor improves after frost. Harvest outer leaves continuously. Plant with dill, beets, onions. Avoid strawberries and beans.
variety_notes: Italian heirloom (16th century). Long narrow dark blue-green savoyed leaves with puckered texture — hence "dinosaur" nickname. Sweeter than curly kale — preferred by most cooks. Cold-hardy to 10F, flavor gets sweeter after frost. Frost-hardy enough to overwinter in zones 6+. Staple for Tuscan ribollita and kale salads.
sources: Johnny's Selected Seeds; Baker Creek; Territorial Seed
source_notes: Multiple names — Lacinato / Dinosaur / Tuscan / Cavolo Nero / Nero di Toscana all refer to the same variety.

disease_resistance: Susceptible to cabbage worms and aphids
companion_notes: Great for baby-leaf salads — harvest young. More tender than other kales even at full size.
variety_notes: Different species (B. napus) from other common kales (B. oleracea) — won't cross with cabbage family. Introduced to North America by Russian traders. Blue-green flat oak-shaped leaves with distinctive red-purple veins. Mild sweet flavor — considered the most tender and easy-to-eat kale. Beautiful ornamental appearance. Faster-maturing than Lacinato.
sources: Johnny's Selected Seeds; Baker Creek; Territorial Seed
source_notes: Different species means it won't cross-pollinate with other brassicas — useful for seed saving.

disease_resistance: Very cold-hardy; standard brassica pest pressure
companion_notes: Exceptional cold hardiness — stands up through heavy frost and snow.
variety_notes: F1 hybrid curly kale with tightly curled blue-green leaves. Extremely cold-hardy — overwinters reliably in zones 6+. Vigorous upright habit. Flavor improves dramatically after frost. Most productive curly kale for long-season harvest. The default commercial curly kale — what you see in grocery stores.
sources: Johnny's Selected Seeds; Territorial Seed
source_notes: Hybrid — won't come true from saved seed. Open-pollinated alternative: Vates.

disease_resistance: Some resistance to blue mold; bolts in heat
companion_notes: Cool-season crop. Plant very early spring (as soon as soil is workable) and fall. Bolts quickly when days lengthen and temps rise.
variety_notes: 1826 heirloom — the oldest American spinach still grown. Thick dark green savoyed (crinkled) leaves with rich flavor. Slow to bolt for a spinach, but still a cool-season crop. Cold-hardy — can overwinter under mulch in zones 5+. Succession plant early spring; stops producing when days exceed 14 hours.
sources: Baker Creek; Territorial Seed; Johnny's Selected Seeds
source_notes: Consider "Tyee" or "Space" F1 hybrids for better disease resistance and bolt resistance if heirloom status not required.

start_method: indoor start 6-8 weeks before last frost
disease_resistance: Susceptible to cabbage worms, aphids, clubroot — rotate out of Brassicas for 3 years
companion_notes: Plant with dill, basil, beets, lettuce, onions, potatoes, spinach. Bad for strawberries and tomatoes. Harvest main head first — then smaller side shoots keep producing for weeks.
variety_notes: Bred at Waltham, Massachusetts in 1950s. Reliable cool-climate broccoli. Medium-large 4-6" tight blue-green main heads followed by side shoots over several weeks. Good side-shoot production is the key feature — one plant yields many cuttings. Cold-hardy. Standard heirloom recommendation.
sources: Johnny's Selected Seeds; Wildrose Heritage; Baker Creek
source_notes: Classic heirloom — reliable but modern hybrids outyield it for commercial growers.

disease_resistance: Susceptible to carrot rust fly, wireworm; generally pest-tolerant
companion_notes: Companion plant with onions, leeks, chives (repel carrot fly) and tomatoes. Avoid dill (can stunt). Loose, rock-free soil 12" deep for straight roots.
variety_notes: Heirloom dating to 1869. Sweet cylindrical 6-7" roots with blunt tips — classic "Nantes" shape. Deep orange with crisp tender flesh. Sweet flavor. Best for fresh eating and juicing. Cool-season crop. Succession-plant spring and fall. Store in ground under mulch in zones 5+.
sources: Johnny's Selected Seeds; Baker Creek; Territorial Seed
source_notes: Nantes type is the sweet-and-tender category — different from Danvers (wedge, storage) or Imperator (long, commercial).

disease_resistance: Good disease resistance; tolerates heavier soil than most carrots
companion_notes: More tolerant of heavy/clay soil than Nantes types. Heat-tolerant.
variety_notes: Heirloom developed in Danvers, MA (1871). Wedge-shaped 6-7" tapered roots with strong tops. Deep orange. Heavier texture than Nantes — better for cooking and storage (6+ months in cold storage). Tolerates heavier soil than most carrots. Heat-tolerant. A classic storage carrot.
sources: Baker Creek; Johnny's Selected Seeds; Territorial Seed
source_notes: Storage capability is the key differentiator from Nantes.

disease_resistance: Generally disease-resistant; watch for leaf miners on greens
companion_notes: Beet "seeds" are actually clusters of 3-6 seeds — thin to one plant per spot. Eat thinnings and tops as greens. Companion with onions, brassicas, lettuce. Avoid pole beans.
variety_notes: 1892 heirloom. Dark red 3-inch round roots with sweet smooth flesh. Perfect shape for canning and roasting. Greens also excellent — chard-like flavor. Tolerates cool and warm temperatures. Reliable across broad range of conditions. The default beet variety for home gardens.
sources: Wildrose Heritage; Baker Creek; Johnny's Selected Seeds
source_notes: Classic American beet — reliable and widely adapted.

disease_resistance: Fast-maturing so minimal pest pressure; flea beetles may damage leaves
companion_notes: Fastest vegetable to maturity — often used as a "row marker" for slower-germinating crops. Succession plant every 2 weeks for continuous supply.
variety_notes: 1949 AAS winner. Round bright red roots with crisp white flesh and mild sweet heat. 22-28 day maturity — ready before most other crops. Excellent in salads. Harvest when 1" diameter — gets pithy if left too long. Succession plant in cool weather (spring and fall). Bolts in heat.
sources: Johnny's Selected Seeds; Burpee; Baker Creek
source_notes: THE beginner vegetable — super fast, super reliable.

disease_resistance: Resistant to rust, fusarium, crown rot — bred specifically for disease resistance
companion_notes: DEDICATE A BED — asparagus lives 15-25 years and shouldn't be moved. Plant crowns 6-8" deep in trench; backfill gradually. No harvest year 1. Light harvest year 2 (2-3 weeks). Full harvest year 3+ (6-8 weeks). Plant with tomatoes, parsley, basil (repels asparagus beetle).
variety_notes: ALL-MALE hybrid — no seed production means more spear production (males put energy into spears, females into seeds). Released by Rutgers University. Large thick dark green spears. Disease resistance bred in — major advantage over heirloom varieties like Mary Washington. Long-term investment: plant once, harvest for 20+ years.
sources: Stark Bros; Johnny's Selected Seeds; Burpee
source_notes: All-male hybrid status is key — Jersey series (Knight, Supreme, Giant) all share this feature.

start_method: plant crowns or divisions in early spring
disease_resistance: Very hardy; minimal pest issues once established
companion_notes: NEVER eat leaves — toxic (oxalic acid). Eat stalks only. No harvest year 1 to establish. Light harvest year 2. Full harvest year 3+. Divide clumps every 5-8 years. Heavy feeder — compost annually. Plant with brassicas (repels pests).
variety_notes: 1837 heirloom — the benchmark rhubarb variety. Large green-red stalks with milder less-tart flavor than modern red-stemmed varieties. Very productive and hardy. Needs cold winter dormancy (zone 3-8 only) — won't thrive in mild climates. Requires fertile well-drained soil. Harvest by pulling stalks (don't cut) — never take more than 1/3 of stalks at once.
sources: Johnny's Selected Seeds; Territorial Seed; Burpee
source_notes: Widely available and reliable; "Canada Red" and "Crimson Cherry" offer redder stalks but less vigor.

start_method: plant crowns or bare roots in spring
disease_resistance: Resistant to verticillium wilt; some tolerance to leaf spot
companion_notes: DAY-NEUTRAL variety — fruits continuously from spring through fall, not a single flush. Plant 12-15" apart. Pinch first flowers year 1 for stronger plants year 2. Replace every 3-4 years as productivity declines. Plant with thyme, borage, lettuce.
variety_notes: Day-neutral breeding from UC Davis. Large bright red firm berries with excellent flavor. Fruits continuously from June through frost. Heat-tolerant — one of the best strawberries for warmer climates. Moderate runner production. Standard for farmers market growers in California.
sources: Johnny's Selected Seeds; Nourse Farms; Stark Bros
source_notes: Three strawberry categories: June-bearing (single summer crop), Ever-bearing (2 crops), Day-neutral (continuous). Day-neutral is most useful for home gardeners.

disease_resistance: Resistant to verticillium wilt, phytophthora crown rot, and anthracnose crown rot
companion_notes: Day-neutral like Seascape. Produces fewer runners than June-bearing types — better for small gardens and raised beds.
variety_notes: Day-neutral release from UC Davis (2006) — now the dominant US commercial day-neutral. Long conical bright red berries with excellent sweet-tart balance. Firm texture — ships well. Superior disease resistance. Productive from June to frost. Most popular home garden day-neutral strawberry.
sources: Johnny's Selected Seeds; Nourse Farms
source_notes: UC Davis-bred; widely regarded as the top day-neutral for flavor and productivity.

disease_resistance: Good general disease resistance; very cold-hardy
companion_notes: June-bearing — single heavy crop in late spring / early summer. Runners need to be controlled or they'll take over. Pinch all flowers year 1 for establishment. Best for freezing and jam due to concentrated harvest.
variety_notes: Released by Cornell University in 1979. Very hardy (zone 3). Bright red large firm berries in a single heavy June crop. Excellent cold tolerance — reliable in northern climates where day-neutrals struggle. Great flavor for jam, freezing, fresh eating. Productive runner formation — easy to propagate.
sources: Nourse Farms; Stark Bros
source_notes: Best June-bearer for cold climates; offers concentrated harvest for preservation.
